library(measure)

    text = element_text(colour = "#222222"),

if (!has_pybaselines) {

}
```

## Introduction

A baseline is the slowly changing background in a measured signal. Baseline
correction estimates that background and subtracts it. The estimate can overlap
real signal features, so inspect the corrected data before using it in later
analysis.

measure includes baseline recipe steps, a custom R callback, and optional access to the Python `pybaselines` library.

## Inspecting baseline variation

The first five spectra from `modeldata::meats` show differences in level and shape. This plot alone does not separate baseline variation from sample composition.

```{r baseline-problem, fig.cap = "Five NIR spectra from modeldata::meats. Color identifies each sample; the x-axis is a channel index and absorbance is unitless.", fig.alt = "Line chart of absorbance by spectral channel index for five meat samples. Colored lines identify samples and show variation in shape and level across the 100 channels."}
data(meats)

# Convert to long format for visualization
meats_viz <- meats |>
  mutate(id = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("x_"),
    names_to = "channel",
    values_to = "transmittance"
  ) |>
  mutate(channel = as.integer(gsub("x_", "", channel)))

# Plot five raw spectra
meats_viz |>
  filter(id <= 5) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = channel, y = transmittance, group = id, color = factor(id))) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Sample ID") +
  labs(
    x = "Spectral channel (index)",
    y = "Absorbance (unitless)",
    title = "Meat spectra before baseline correction"
  ) +
  article_plot_theme
```

Differences between spectra may reflect baseline variation, sample composition, or both. The plot does not identify their source.

## Built-in baseline correction methods

### Asymmetric least squares (ALS)

`step_measure_baseline_als()` estimates an asymmetric least-squares baseline for each spectrum and subtracts it from the signal. The example uses `lambda = 1e6` and `p = 0.01`; inspect the corrected trace before selecting parameters for other data.

```{r als-baseline, fig.cap = "One meat spectrum before and after ALS correction with lambda = 1e6 and p = 0.01. Both traces use the same 100 spectral channels.", fig.alt = "Overlay line chart of one meat sample's absorbance across 100 channel indices before and after ALS correction. The raw trace sits well above the corrected trace; both retain a broad peak around channel 60."}
rec_als <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_baseline_als(lambda = 1e6, p = 0.01)

processed_als <- bake(prep(rec_als), new_data = NULL)

raw_als <- meats |>
  slice(1) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("x_"),
    names_to = "feature",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    location = as.integer(sub("^x_", "", feature)),
    value,
    processing = "Raw"
  )

corrected_als <- processed_als |>
  slice(1) |>
  unnest(.measures) |>
  transmute(location, value, processing = "ALS corrected")

bind_rows(raw_als, corrected_als) |>
  mutate(processing = factor(processing, levels = c("Raw", "ALS corrected"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = location, y = value, colour = processing)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    name = "Processing",
    values = c("Raw" = "#6B7280", "ALS corrected" = "#0072B2")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Spectral channel (index)",
    y = "Absorbance (unitless)",
    title = "ALS correction of one meat spectrum"
  ) +
  article_plot_theme
```

**Key parameters:**

- `lambda`: Smoothness penalty (higher = smoother baseline). Try 10^4 to 10^9.
- `p`: Asymmetry parameter (0-1). Lower values fit below the signal. Try 0.001-0.1.

### Polynomial baseline

`step_measure_baseline_poly()` fits a polynomial across the spectrum and subtracts the fitted curve. The example uses degree 2; inspect the corrected signal to check whether the fit has altered features relevant to your analysis.

```{r poly-baseline, fig.cap = "One meat spectrum before and after degree-2 polynomial baseline correction. Both traces use the same 100 spectral channels.", fig.alt = "Overlay line chart of one meat sample's absorbance across 100 channel indices before and after degree-2 polynomial correction. The raw trace sits well above the corrected trace, which fluctuates around zero and retains a broad peak around channel 60."}
rec_poly <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_baseline_poly(degree = 2)

processed_poly <- bake(prep(rec_poly), new_data = NULL)

raw_poly <- meats |>
  slice(1) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("x_"),
    names_to = "feature",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    location = as.integer(sub("^x_", "", feature)),
    value,
    processing = "Raw"
  )

corrected_poly <- processed_poly |>
  slice(1) |>
  unnest(.measures) |>
  transmute(location, value, processing = "Polynomial corrected")

bind_rows(raw_poly, corrected_poly) |>
  mutate(processing = factor(processing, levels = c("Raw", "Polynomial corrected"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = location, y = value, colour = processing)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    name = "Processing",
    values = c("Raw" = "#6B7280", "Polynomial corrected" = "#0072B2")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Spectral channel (index)",
    y = "Absorbance (unitless)",
    title = "Polynomial correction of one meat spectrum"
  ) +
  article_plot_theme
```

### Robust fitting baseline

`step_measure_baseline_rf()` estimates a baseline with locally weighted regression and iterative reweighting. Check its fit on spectra with the signal shapes and noise levels in your data.

```{r rf-baseline}
rec_rf <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_baseline_rf(span = 0.5) |>
  step_measure_output_wide(prefix = "nir_")

processed_rf <- bake(prep(rec_rf), new_data = NULL)
```

### Detrending

`step_measure_detrend()` removes polynomial trends from spectra. The simplest baseline correction - just removes the overall trend.

```{r detrend}
rec_detrend <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_detrend(degree = 1) |>
  step_measure_output_wide(prefix = "nir_")

processed_detrend <- bake(prep(rec_detrend), new_data = NULL)
```

### GPC/SEC baseline correction

The core `step_measure_baseline_gpc()` has been superseded. For SEC/GPC data,
use `measure.sec::step_sec_baseline()`, which is maintained in the companion
package. The synthetic example runs when `measure.sec` is installed; it is
skipped with a message otherwise.

```{r gpc-baseline}
sec_data <- tibble::tibble(
  sample_id = rep(1:3, each = 20),
  concentration = rep(c(10, 25, 50), each = 20),
  time = rep(seq(0, 19), 3),
  signal = rep(
    seq(0.1, 0.2, length.out = 20) +
      c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0.3, rep(0, 10)),
    3
  ) + rep(c(0, 0.1, 0.2), each = 20)
)

if (requireNamespace("measure.sec", quietly = TRUE)) {
  sec_fit <- recipe(concentration ~ ., data = sec_data) |>
    update_role(sample_id, new_role = "id") |>
    step_measure_input_long(
      signal,
      location = vars(time),
      col_name = "ri"
    ) |>
    measure.sec::step_sec_baseline(
      measures = "ri",
      left_frac = 0.1,
      right_frac = 0.1
    ) |>
    prep()

  bake(sec_fit, new_data = NULL) |>
    dplyr::select(sample_id, concentration)
} else {
  message("SEC example skipped: install the optional measure.sec package.")
}
```

## Custom baseline functions

`step_measure_baseline_custom()` lets you provide any R function for baseline estimation. Your function receives a `measure_tbl` (tibble with `location` and `value` columns) and should return a numeric vector of baseline values.

### Using a function

```{r custom-function}
# Simple moving minimum baseline
moving_min_baseline <- function(x, window = 51) {
  y <- x$value
  n <- length(y)
  baseline <- numeric(n)
  half_win <- window %/% 2


  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    start <- max(1, i - half_win)
    end <- min(n, i + half_win)
    baseline[i] <- min(y[start:end], na.rm = TRUE)
  }
  baseline
}

rec_custom <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_baseline_custom(.fn = moving_min_baseline, window = 101) |>
  step_measure_output_wide(prefix = "nir_")

processed_custom <- bake(prep(rec_custom), new_data = NULL)
```

### Using a formula

For quick one-liners, use the formula interface where `.x` is the `measure_tbl`:

```{r custom-formula}
# LOESS baseline using formula
rec_loess <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_baseline_custom(
    .fn = ~ stats::loess(.x$value ~ .x$location, span = span)$fitted,
    span = 0.3
  ) |>
  step_measure_output_wide(prefix = "nir_")

processed_loess <- bake(prep(rec_loess), new_data = NULL)
```

### Extracting the baseline

With `step_measure_baseline_custom()` and `step_measure_baseline_py()`, set `subtract = FALSE` to get the baseline itself instead of the corrected signal:

```{r extract-baseline}
# Use custom baseline with subtract = FALSE to extract the baseline
rec_extract <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_baseline_custom(
    .fn = ~ stats::loess(.x$value ~ .x$location, span = 0.5)$fitted,
    subtract = FALSE
  )

baselines <- bake(prep(rec_extract), new_data = NULL)

# The .measures column now contains the estimated baselines
baselines |>
  slice(1) |>
  unnest(.measures) |>
  head()
```

## Python pybaselines integration

`step_measure_baseline_py()` calls baseline methods from the Python
[pybaselines](https://pybaselines.readthedocs.io/) library.

### Setup

First, make reticulate available in R and declare pybaselines for the Python
environment used by reticulate. These commands are for you to run when you want
to use the backend. The availability check initializes the selected Python
runtime; reticulate may create a managed environment according to its
configuration. measure preserves an explicitly selected interpreter:

```r
if (!requireNamespace("reticulate", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("reticulate")
}
reticulate::py_require("pybaselines")
```

### Using pybaselines methods

```{r pybaselines-example, eval = has_pybaselines}
py_small <- meats[1:5, ]
rec_py <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = py_small) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_baseline_py(method = "asls", lam = 1e6, p = 0.01) |>
  step_measure_output_wide(prefix = "nir_")

py_fit <- prep(rec_py)
py_processed <- bake(py_fit, new_data = NULL)
py_processed[, 1:6]
```

### Available pybaselines methods

| Category | Methods |
|----------|---------|
| Whittaker | `asls`, `iasls`, `airpls`, `arpls`, `drpls`, `psalsa` |
| Polynomial | `poly`, `modpoly`, `imodpoly`, `loess`, `quant_reg` |
| Morphological | `mor`, `imor`, `rolling_ball`, `tophat` |
| Spline | `pspline_asls`, `pspline_airpls`, `mixture_model` |
| Smooth | `snip`, `swima`, `noise_median` |
| Classification | `dietrich`, `golotvin`, `fastchrom` |

See the [pybaselines documentation](https://pybaselines.readthedocs.io/) for the full list and parameter details.

## Using derivatives for baseline correction

Savitzky-Golay derivatives can reduce constant or linear baseline components. Derivatives also change the signal scale and can change peak shapes, so inspect them before interpretation.

```{r sg-baseline}
# A first derivative suppresses a constant offset
rec_d1 <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_savitzky_golay(window_side = 7, differentiation_order = 1) |>
  step_measure_output_wide(prefix = "nir_")

# A second derivative suppresses a linear trend
rec_d2 <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_savitzky_golay(window_side = 7, differentiation_order = 2) |>
  step_measure_output_wide(prefix = "nir_")
```

## Choosing a method

| Method | Operation | Tunable | Notes |
|--------|-----------|---------|-------|
| `step_measure_baseline_als()` | Estimates and subtracts an asymmetric least-squares baseline | Yes | Tune `lambda` and `p` for the signal |
| `step_measure_baseline_poly()` | Fits and subtracts a polynomial | Yes | `degree` sets polynomial order |
| `step_measure_baseline_rf()` | Fits a locally weighted baseline | Yes | `span` controls the local fit |
| `step_measure_detrend()` | Removes a polynomial trend | Yes | `degree` sets trend order |
| `measure.sec::step_sec_baseline()` | Processes SEC/GPC traces | No | Provided by the companion package |
| `step_measure_baseline_custom()` | Calls a supplied R function | Optional | The function returns baseline values |
| `step_measure_baseline_py()` | Calls a pybaselines method | Yes | Requires the Python backend |
| `step_measure_savitzky_golay()` | Smooths or differentiates signals | Yes | Derivatives change signal scale |

## Hyperparameter tuning

Most baseline correction steps are tunable with the tidymodels tuning framework:

```{r tuning-example}
rec_tunable <- recipe(water ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  step_measure_baseline_als(
    lambda = tune::tune(),
    p = tune::tune()
  ) |>
  step_measure_output_wide(prefix = "nir_")

tune::tunable(rec_tunable)
```

`step_measure_baseline_custom()` can expose callback arguments to the tuning
framework. Declare a parameter in `tunable`, capture `tune::tune()` in the
matching callback argument, then extract and finalize it through the public
tuning API:

```{r tunable-custom}
rec_custom_tuned <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats_long) |>
  update_role(id, new_role = "id") |>
  step_measure_input_long(transmittance, location = vars(channel)) |>
  step_measure_baseline_custom(
    .fn = ~ {
      fit <- lm(.x$value ~ poly(.x$location, degree))
      predict(fit)
    },
    degree = tune::tune(id = "baseline_degree"),
    tunable = list(
      degree = list(
        pkg = "dials",
        fun = "degree_int",
        range = c(1L, 5L)
      )
    )
  )

custom_parameters <- tune::extract_parameter_set_dials(rec_custom_tuned)
custom_parameters

rec_custom_final <- tune::finalize_recipe(
  rec_custom_tuned,
  list(baseline_degree = 2L)
)

rec_custom_fixed <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats_long) |>
  update_role(id, new_role = "id") |>
  step_measure_input_long(transmittance, location = vars(channel)) |>
  step_measure_baseline_custom(
    .fn = ~ {
      fit <- lm(.x$value ~ poly(.x$location, degree))
      predict(fit)
    },
    degree = 2L
  )

all.equal(
  bake(prep(rec_custom_final), new_data = NULL)$.measures,
  bake(prep(rec_custom_fixed), new_data = NULL)$.measures
)
```

## Complete preprocessing pipeline

This recipe combines baseline estimation, sample-wise normalization, and a
first derivative. Each step changes the signal, so inspect intermediate output
when deciding whether the sequence suits the analysis:

```{r complete-pipeline}
rec_complete <- recipe(water + fat + protein ~ ., data = meats) |>
  step_measure_input_wide(starts_with("x_")) |>
  # Baseline correction
  step_measure_baseline_als(lambda = 1e6, p = 0.01) |>
  # Scatter correction
  step_measure_snv() |>
  # Smoothing with mild derivative
  step_measure_savitzky_golay(window_side = 5, differentiation_order = 1) |>
  # Output for modeling
  step_measure_output_wide(prefix = "nir_")

final_data <- bake(prep(rec_complete), new_data = NULL)
final_data[1:5, 1:8]
```
